thread.title: The Jewish PRIZE - Commentary Magazine

author: Jeffrey Lax
title: The Jewish PRIZE - Commentary Magazine
text:
Over the past half decade—well before the horrific Hamas attacks of October 7, 2023—anti-Semitic incidents have surged across the United States, in workplaces, universities, public institutions, K–12 schools, and everyday life. Jewish individuals have faced harassment, exclusion, hostile environments, and retaliation, often disguised as political opposition to “Zionism.” Yet political Zionism, in the sense of a movement seeking the creation of a Jewish state, has not existed for more than a century. It achieved its goal in 1948. Political Zionism also never existed in the thousands of years of Jewish history that preceded Theodor Herzl. For Jews, Zionism is not—and has never been—a political ideology. It is ancestral, it is cultural, it is often religious; and in all of these cases, it is an integral expression of Jewish identity. Courageous advocates, journalists, and organizations have done vital work exposing this hatred: exposing the meaning of chants such as “Globalize the intifada,” condemning exclusion from professional spaces, fighting compelled speech in unions, and outing glaring double standards in institutional responses. This exposure has been indispensable.
But something in this fight has always been missing. Even in sympathetic venues—among litigators, policymakers, and administrators—advocates too often falter at the point of precision. They condemn anti-Semitism without rigorously defining the Jewish identities it targets or mapping those identities onto the protected categories of American law. The consequences have been tangible setbacks in federal court under Title VI and Title VII, from the First Circuit’s affirmation of dismissal in Stand With Us v. MIT (2025) to dismissals and narrow rulings in cases nationwide.
This imprecision is not merely tactical. It reflects a deeper failure to articulate a fundamental truth: Jews are a people whose identity encompasses religion, ethnicity, ancestry, culture, and a profound—often faith-inflected—connection to the Land of Israel and its people. The solution to this imprecision is a new framework that the Jewish community and others can adopt to make it clear both to themselves and to those who are not of Jewish origin what Jewishness is. I call it PRIZE.
PRIZE identifies the five distinct ways Jews experience and express their identity. Each category aligns directly with protected characteristics under Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (race, color, national origin), Title VII (religion, race, national origin), and analogous state and local laws.
P.R.I.Z.E. stands for:
- Practiced Judaism (religion)
- Religious Zionism (faith-based connection to the Land of Israel)
- Israeli nationality
- Zionist ethnicity (shared cultural, historical, and ancestral ties to the Land of Israel and its people)
- Ethnic Jewish identity (broader ancestral, cultural, and peoplehood dimensions)
These categories are not invented; they describe empirical reality.
An individual may belong to one, several, or all five categories. A secular Jew with Eastern European roots and a deep cultural attachment to Israel embodies Ethnic Jewish identity (“E”) and Zionist ethnicity (“Z”). A religious Jew who sees the connection to the Land through a biblical lens adds Practiced Judaism (“P”) and Religious Zionism (“R”). An Israeli American includes Israeli nationality (“I”).
PRIZE captures this complexity without forcing Jews into a single box or tying identity to any particular Israeli government policy. None of the five categories depends on attitudes toward the Israeli government at all; they rest on Jews’ lived connections—to the land (not the government), to the people, to ancestry, culture, and faith.
Recent legal cases illustrate how the absence of the precise definition offered by my PRIZE formula undermines otherwise strong claims.
_____________
In Stand With Us v. MIT, Jewish students alleged that MIT failed to address a hostile educational environment under Title VI amid post–October 7 protests and encampments that restricted campus access. The First Circuit affirmed dismissal in a 54-page opinion in October 2025. The complaint by Stand With Us delved deeply into the Gaza conflict and Israeli policies and, in so doing, implicitly relied on the so-called IHRA definition, the painstakingly negotiated 2016 document that seeks to provide a consensus delineation of what anti-Semitism is. Now, I fully support the IHRA definition in international, geopolitical, UN, and many moral and educational contexts. It has played a valuable role worldwide in identifying and combating hatred, including complex forms of discrimination.
However, in U.S. domestic civil rights litigation, heavy reliance on IHRA in pleadings carries risks and has proved problematic. It can entangle claims in foreign policy debates that courts prefer to avoid. I raise this point specifically in the context of Stand With Us v. MIT because, although the plaintiffs did not cite or plead the IHRA definition itself, their core arguments relied heavily on several of its key “contemporary examples”—including applying double standards to Israel, calling the Jewish state “genocidal” or a “racist endeavor,” drawing comparisons of Israeli policy to Nazi behavior, and using anti-Zionist rhetoric to deny the Jewish people’s right to self-determination.
These are worthy aims, but they are not the way to win in court. A PRIZE-centered approach would have grounded every claim in the plaintiffs’ specific protected identities. It would have emphasized the defendants’ interference with Ethnic Jewish Identity, through denial of ancestral peoplehood and targeted harassment of students simply because they were Jewish. It would have cited their rejection of Zionist ethnicity (through hostility to their cultural and historical ties to the Land and of Israel and its people), and their effort to interfere with Practiced Judaism (through direct disruption of religious observance). One especially compelling example was the blocking of a Passover Seder: The pro-Palestinian encampments were deliberately positioned directly across from MIT’s Hillel House, making it impossible for observant Jewish students to hold this sacred religious gathering on campus. This interference was not abstract political speech—it was concrete, targeted, and disruptive of a core religious practice. Instead of thoroughly developing these protected-class harms and showing the court exactly how the defendants’ conduct violated specific PRIZE dimensions of Jewish identity, the plaintiffs spent disproportionate time on geopolitical arguments and IHRA-style examples—a missed opportunity that left the complaint vulnerable.
In any case, the First Circuit’s opinion in the matter revealed a greater institutional reluctance to involve itself in the dispute. The court framed virtually the entire controversy as a clash of protected First Amendment speech, giving short shrift to the reality of discriminatory harassing conduct and weeks-long (in some cases months-long) physical encampments and obstructions that went far beyond mere words. Such targeted harassment and sustained interference with Jewish students’ access to education do not and should not automatically receive First Amendment shelter. A court confronting clear patterns of severe and pervasive harassment should have recognized actionable discrimination, rather than reflexively prioritizing political speech over the lived experience of targeted Jewish students on an American campus. That said, the court might have viewed matters differently had the plaintiffs used the PRIZE framework.
In the case of Goldstein v. CUNY (May 2026), which involves the alleged harassment and discrimination of Zionist Jewish professors at Borough of Manhattan Community College, Judge Jeannette Vargas struck extensive historical allegations about the State of Israel from biblical times onward as irrelevant and prejudicial. The case was recently dismissed by the same judge.
PRIZE avoids the trap of extensive historical pleading entirely. It would advise against reciting the political or military history of the modern State of Israel. Instead, it describes the lived, protected dimensions of Jewish identity itself—including the ancient, continuous ancestral and cultural connection that predates any modern government. This is akin to recognizing Italian Americans’ ties to Italy or Native Americans’ ties to ancestral lands. One is irrelevant geopolitics; the other is core to defining membership in a protected class.
_____________
My own litigation against CUNY provides a powerful demonstration of PRIZE’s effectiveness in practice. A 2021 determination by the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) found reasonable cause that CUNY had discriminated and retaliated against observant Jewish faculty on the basis of religion and failed to take corrective action. This foundation enabled a major victory in New York State Supreme Court.
In August 2023, Judge Gina Abadi denied CUNY’s motion to dismiss the discrimination, hostile work environment, and retaliation claims under employment law both in New York City and New York State in nearly all respects. By grounding the claims squarely in the protected category of Practiced Judaism (religion)—and meticulously detailing how CUNY condoned and exacerbated the discrimination—the PRIZE-aligned pleading produced strikingly strong judicial findings. The court expressly held “that plaintiffs adequately allege that they were discriminated against because of their religion and that CUNY, in response to the alleged discriminatory conduct, failed to take corrective action, thereby creating a hostile working environment.”
Judge Abadi repeatedly rejected CUNY’s attempts to evade liability, emphasizing that the complaint sufficiently pled severe or pervasive conduct that altered the conditions of employment and that CUNY’s own inaction supported liability for condonation. The motion to dismiss all claims (for all but one unrelated moot claim by one plaintiff) was denied, in a devastating blow to CUNY.
Settlements achieved by groups like the Brandeis Center, requiring explicit policy protections for Zionist-identified employees and students, demonstrate the advantage of precision and underscore the potential for success when enforcement focuses on protected-class harm. Additional Title VII examples in corporate and academic workplaces—such as exclusion from DEI initiatives treating Jewish or Zionist ethnicity as disqualifying—show how PRIZE transforms disputes into classic disparate-treatment or hostile-environment claims under both statutes.
In each instance, courts emphasize the need for plaintiffs to connect adverse actions directly to a protected characteristic; PRIZE supplies that connection consistently and effectively. These patterns repeat across the country, from federal district courts handling campus cases to EEOC administrative proceedings involving faculty and staff. Vague pleadings framed as general “anti-Semitism” or political disagreement frequently fail. PRIZE supplies the precise link that courts demand.
